procedural_history.originating_court: First Appellant (likely a government official) passed an order dated November 20, 1961, under Section 15 of the Bombay Land Requisition Act.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated November 20, 1961, passed by the first appellant under Section 15 of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, requisitioning land for a new village site for flood victims.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondents (landowners) filed a Special Civil Application No. 373 of 1961 in the Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench, challenging the validity of the requisition order. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order, holding that the Act did not authorize requisitioning for a permanent purpose like establishing a new village site.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants (Collector, Akola) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment and order dated August 28, 1962. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and remanded the matter to the High Court to decide the other questions raised in the petition that it had not previously addressed.

directions: The order passed by the High Court is set aside.
The matter is remanded to the High Court to decide the other questions raised in the petition in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the power to requisition land under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, a temporary statute, can be exercised for a public purpose that is not temporary in nature.

facts: The government requisitioned land under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, a temporary statute, for the public purpose of establishing a new village to resettle flood victims.
The landowners challenged the order, arguing that a temporary law could not be used for a permanent purpose like building a new village.
The High Court agreed with the landowners and quashed the requisition order, reasoning that the temporary nature of the Act implied that it could only be used for temporary purposes.
law: The relevant law is Section 5(1) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, which states that the government may requisition "any land for any public purpose."
The Act itself was a temporary statute, meaning it was in force for a limited period and required extensions to remain active.
application: The Supreme Court performed a plain reading of Section 5(1) and found that the words "for any public purpose" were wide enough to include any public purpose, whether temporary or permanent.

The Court held that the High Court was wrong to infer a limitation on the *nature* of the purpose from the *temporary duration* of the Act. It stated that this was to "confound the temporary life of the statute with the character of the purpose for which the power thereunder can be exercised."

The Court found no inherent conflict or "antithesis" between the power to requisition (temporary taking) and the power of acquisition (permanent taking). It noted that the government could use the requisition power to meet an emergency and later initiate proceedings for permanent acquisition under a different law.

The only limitation on the power, according to the Court, is that the purpose must be a public one. The decision on how best to use the requisitioned land, and the potential consequences of having to return it later, rests with the government, not the courts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the power to requisition land under the temporary Bombay Land Requisition Act can be exercised for any public purpose, regardless of whether that purpose is temporary or permanent. The temporary nature of the statute does not restrict the scope of the public purpose for which the power can be used. Therefore, the requisition for establishing a new village was valid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power to requisition land under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, a temporary statute, can be exercised for a public purpose that is not temporary in nature.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's interpretation of section 5(1) of the Act was incorrect.
The Act authorizes an order of requisitioning even if the public purpose for which it is made is not temporary.
The only requirement of section 5(1) is that the requisition is for a "public purpose," and it does not impose a condition that the purpose must also be temporary in nature.
respondent_arguments: Since the Act is a temporary statute, the power to requisition land under it can only be exercised for a temporary purpose.
An order passed for a permanent purpose, such as establishing a new village site for flood victims, could not have been in the contemplation of the temporary Act.
Exercising the power for a permanent purpose would amount to an abuse of the Act, as it would render impossible the operation of other sections (like the one for returning the land).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power to requisition land under a statute for "any public purpose" is not implicitly restricted to temporary public purposes, even if the statute itself has a limited duration. The temporary life of the statute does not limit the character of the public purpose for which the power can be exercised.
obiter: It is for the requisitioning authority to judge and not for a court of law to decide how best the land is to be used.

If the requisitioning authority uses the land for a purpose which is not temporary, it is for the Government and those who put up structures to contemplate the possibility of having to return the land to the owner in its original state.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's view is that the temporary nature of the Bombay Land Requisition Act does not restrict the exercise of its powers to only temporary public purposes. The court found that reading such a limitation into the Act would be to confuse the temporary life of the statute itself with the character of the purpose for which the power can be exercised. The plain language of section 5(1) allows for requisitioning for "any public purpose," which is wide enough to include purposes that are not temporary in nature.
legal_tests_applied: Plain reading of a statute: The court analyzed the plain meaning of the words in section 5(1) of the Act, noting that "On the face of it the sub-section does not contain any express limitation to the power to requisition, the only limitation being that an order thereunder can be passed for a public purpose only."
why_respondent_won: The words 'for any public purpose' in s. 5(1) are wide enough to include any purpose of whatsoever nature and do not contain any restriction regarding the nature of that purpose. It places no limitation on the competent authority as to what kind of public purpose it should be for the valid exercise of its power nor does it confine the exercise of that power to a purpose which is a temporary one.

To read into the section a limitation that the purpose contemplated by it is only temporary is to confound the temporary life of the statute with the character of the purpose for which the power thereunder can be exercised.

Section 9, which provides for the return of the land upon derequisition, has nothing to do with the nature or character of the purpose for which the land was requisitioned. The land must revert to the owner as soon as it is released, whatever use it has been put to during the period of requisitioning.
The life of the power (i.e., the temporary duration of the Act) and the purpose for which it is exercised are two distinct ingredients of section 5(1) and ought not to be confused.
